title: B/1/2165's Base64 Logit Mode
takeaway: In the second model's dictionary, the feature that matches the base64 feature does the same thing to the output that the original does: its logit-weight histogram has a small second mode, centered near +0.32, made almost entirely of tokens that would continue a base64 string. This is the downstream half of the universality claim — the two features do not just fire on the same text, they push up the same vocabulary.
walkthrough:
### What is plotted

One histogram over the whole vocabulary. A [[logit-weight]] is what you get by pushing a feature's direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding: one number per vocabulary entry, saying how much that entry's next-token logit rises when the feature fires. The plot bins those numbers for a single feature, B/1/2165.

The horizontal axis is that weight, $-0.6$ to $+0.6$. Because softmax is shift-invariant there is no absolute zero, so each feature's weights are shifted until their median is $0$ (see [[logit-weight-median-centering]]). The vertical axis, "Density", is a smoothed count of vocabulary entries; only relative area means anything.

### How the color works

Every column is stacked and shaded by a [[computational-proxy]] applied to the token itself. The proxy is a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]]: $\log\!\big(P(t\mid\text{base64})/P(t)\big)$. The numerator treats base64 as characters drawn uniformly from a 64-symbol alphabet ([[base64-proxy]]); the denominator is the token's plain unigram frequency ([[unigram-p-s-estimate]]). Deep blue is $-5$, deep red is $+5$.

So red means: this token is far likelier inside a random base64 string than in ordinary text. Those are the tokens that would continue a base64 string.

The narrow strip under the plot is the same data with every column stretched to full height — the composition at each weight, ignoring how many tokens are there.

### What it shows

The bulk is one tall mode, peaking near $0.27\text{M}$ at a weight of about $+0.02$, and it is solid blue. The paper reads this mass as [[weight-interference]]: noise the feature is forced to carry because directions in superposition are not orthogonal, not deliberate prediction.

The inset magnifies the box from $0.20$ to $0.60$. The curve dips to a trough around $0.27$, then rises again into [[logit-weight-second-mode]] peaking near $+0.32$ — roughly a twentieth as tall as the main mode — and dying out by about $0.45$.

Reading the color across that stretch: at $0.205$ about three-fifths of the column is still blue, at $0.27$ about a sixth, and at the peak essentially none. The transition is gradual rather than a clean break, which the paper attributes to base64 tokens also occurring in ordinary text.

Since B/1/2165 was picked only for firing when A/1/2357 fires, matching logit modes is separate evidence for [[feature-universality]].

terms.definition: The chart title. It says the figure is a histogram whose data points are the individual logit weights of one feature, one per vocabulary entry.
The feature being plotted. Read the notation as model B, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 2165 within that run.
The base64 feature from the first model, named in the sentence that introduces this figure. B/1/2165 is its counterpart, and this figure exists to show the two behave alike downstream.

The amount a token's next-token logit changes per unit of the feature's activation, computed along the linear path from the feature direction through the MLP output weights, a linearized layer norm, and the unembedding.
The figure's own gloss on the axis. It names the quantity as a weight on a path, not a measured effect on real data.
A smoothed count of how many vocabulary entries fall at each logit weight. It is a kernel density scaled to counts, so the absolute values are only meaningful relative to each other.

terms.term: "Distribution of weights from feature to logit for each vocab element" (subtitle)
terms.definition: States the population being histogrammed: one weight per vocabulary element, not per dataset token.
One entry of the model's token vocabulary. Extremely rare or never-used entries are dropped from these plots.
The colour variable. For each token it is the log of how much likelier that token is under the base64 hypothesis than under ordinary text.

terms.term: "base64 vs token unigram distribuiton" (legend subtitle, typo in the original)
terms.definition: Names the two distributions in the ratio: base64 as the hypothesis in the numerator, the corpus-wide per-token unigram distribution as the baseline in the denominator.
An encoding that writes arbitrary bytes as characters from the 64-symbol alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. Here it is modelled as a string of characters drawn uniformly from that alphabet.

In this figure, a vocabulary entry that would plausibly come next inside a base64 string — short mixed-case alphanumeric fragments that occur far more often per character in base64 than in ordinary text.

terms.term: Blue end of the colour bar
terms.definition: Log-likelihood ratio at or below -5: tokens much likelier in ordinary text than in a base64 string.

terms.term: Red end of the colour bar
terms.definition: Log-likelihood ratio at or above +5: tokens that essentially only appear inside base64 strings.
The tall blue hump centred just above zero, holding almost the entire vocabulary. The paper reads it as interference rather than intended prediction.
The small bump in the right tail. It is the set of tokens the feature actively pushes up, and here it is made of base64 tokens.

A magnification of the region of the main plot from logit weight 0.20 to 0.60 and density 0 to roughly 44K, connected to the main axes by dotted lines. It exists because the second mode is invisible at the main plot's vertical scale.

terms.term: Conditional strip (band below the main plot)
terms.definition: The same stacked colours with every column stretched to full height, so it shows the mix of proxy values at each logit weight independently of how many tokens sit there.
Five labels in the inset, each attached by a thin vertical line to a particular logit weight, sampling which vocabulary entries live at that point in the distribution.

The tokens sampled at the left edge of the zoom, around weight 0.22. They are alphanumeric but also ordinary English fragments ('ixel' from pixel, 'avascript' from JavaScript), which is why the column there is still mostly blue.

The tokens sampled just past the peak of the second mode, around weight 0.35. Nearly all are two-character mixed-case fragments of the kind a BPE tokenizer produces on random base64, and the column there is uniformly red.
The tokens sampled on the falling right side of the second mode, around weight 0.44 — the same character-pair pattern, at the weights the feature pushes hardest.
Two labels at the extreme right of the zoom, near weights 0.50 and 0.54, where the density has fallen almost to the axis. These are the individual tokens the feature up-weights most.

The paper's name for logit weights a feature carries without meaning to, because features are packed into more directions than the space has dimensions and so are not orthogonal. It is the proposed explanation for the large central mode.
Softmax only cares about logit differences, so logit weights have no absolute scale; the paper subtracts each feature's median weight to fix one.
A cheaply computed score standing in for the hypothesis about what a feature is for, used here as an independent label on tokens rather than as a fit to the feature.

The question of whether separately trained models learn the same features. B/1/2165 was found by looking for the feature in run B/1 whose activations correlate most with A/1/2357's, so its logit weights are a second, independent test.

numbers.meaning: The plotted range of the horizontal logit-weight axis, with ticks every 0.1. The range is a display choice; weights outside it, if any, are not shown.
The labelled density ticks. Since density here is a smoothed count over vocabulary entries, the area under the curve is on the order of the vocabulary size rather than 1.
The height of the main mode at its peak, read off the plot. It is where the great majority of vocabulary entries sit.
The logit weight at which the main mode peaks, read off the plot. It sits just above zero because the weights are centred on their median, not their mode.
The median logit weight, by construction: the paper shifts every feature's weights so the median lands here.
The horizontal span of the region the inset magnifies, marked in the main plot by a dotted rectangle.
The top of the magnified box in density units, roughly a sixth of the main peak. Everything in the inset is smaller than this.
The logit weight where the curve bottoms out between the two modes, read off the plot. It is the dip that makes the second mode a separate mode rather than a shoulder.
The logit weight at the peak of the second mode, read off the plot. This is the figure's main location claim: the base64 tokens cluster here.
The density at the second mode's peak, read off the plot — roughly one twentieth, about 5%, of the main mode's peak height. The second mode is a small population.
Where the second mode has fallen back to near the axis, read off the plot. Beyond it only a thin sliver of tokens remains out to 0.6.
The approximate logit weights the five token labels point to, measured from the leader lines. They walk from the transition zone, through the peak, out to the extreme tail.
How many tokens each of the five labels lists. The counts shrink toward the right because there are fewer tokens out there to name.

The ticks on the colour bar, in log-likelihood-ratio units. The scale is clipped at both ends, so a token at 5 is at least that base64-specific and may be far more so; the paper does not state the log base.
A token equally likely under the base64 model and under the ordinary unigram distribution. The white middle of the bar is the neutral point.

The fraction of each column that is blue at weights 0.205, 0.25, 0.27 and 0.32, measured off the image. It quantifies the gradual handover from ordinary tokens to base64 tokens as you move right, rather than a sharp boundary.

The probability the proxy assigns to each character of a base64 string, one over the size of the base64 alphabet [a-zA-Z0-9+/]. A token's probability under the base64 hypothesis is this raised to its character length.

The probability the proxy assigns to a character outside the base64 alphabet. One space or punctuation mark in a token therefore drives its ratio far negative, which is why the main mode is uniformly deep blue.

The activation correlation between A/1/2357 and B/1/2165 reported in the surrounding text. It is how B/1/2165 was identified as the counterpart, and it involves no logit weights — which is what makes this figure independent evidence.

The median activation correlation between an A/1 feature and its closest B/1 match, from the paper's global universality analysis. It is the yardstick against which the 0.85 for this pair counts as high.
